vignette:
Presenting Narrative

Thomas is a 74-year-old man who has lived alone for the past twelve years. He works as a freelance editor, specializing in historical memoirs and academic manuscripts. His apartment in a coastal town is neat, quiet, and orderly. He keeps the blinds drawn most of the day.

The marriage ended in 2012, but the pain began decades earlier. Thomas met his ex-wife, Eleanor, in the late 1970s at a publishing house in Auckland. She was a graphic designer, sharp and magnetic. He was a junior editor. They married quickly, and for the first few years, Thomas remembers a kind of breathless happiness. The first incident happened three years in, after a dinner party. Eleanor accused him of flirting with a colleague. She slapped him across the face, hard. He was stunned, but she cried immediately, apologized, and said she was just so in love with him she couldn't bear the thought of losing him. He believed her. He stayed.

Over the next thirty years, the violence became a rhythm. It was never daily, but it was predictable. It would follow a pattern: a period of tension, a sharp comment from Thomas, an explosion from Eleanor. The worst times were when she threw things—books, a ceramic mug, once a heavy glass ashtray that caught him on the temple. He learned to stand still, to make himself small. He learned to read the temperature of a room by the set of her jaw. He learned that if he apologized quickly enough, if he absorbed the blame completely, the storm would pass sooner.

Thomas never told anyone. Not his brother, not his doctor. He was an editor, a man of words, but he had no language for what was happening. He felt a deep, corroding shame. He told himself it was his fault, that he was too sensitive, too passive, that he provoked her. He edited his life the way he edited manuscripts: cutting the painful passages, smoothing over the rough edges, making it presentable for public view. He stayed in the marriage for the children, he told himself. But the children grew up and left, and he stayed anyway, a ghost in his own house, walking on eggshells until his bones ached.

The divorce was her idea. She found someone else. Thomas signed the papers without a fight. He moved into this small apartment and thought he would finally be free. He thought the silence would be a relief.

It is not a relief. The silence is the worst part.

Now, at seventy-four, Thomas cannot sit still. He edits on his laptop for hours, sometimes through the night, because if he stops, the memories come in a flood. He hears her voice in the supermarket, in the quiet of his own kitchen. He startles at the sound of a dropped book. He has not had a romantic relationship since the divorce. He cannot imagine letting anyone close enough to touch him. He flinches when the mailman knocks. He avoids crowds because he feels a constant, low-level vigilance, scanning for the flash of anger in another person's face.

He has nightmares, but they are not of the violence. They are of the waiting—the hours before the explosion, the terrible quiet when he knew something was coming but could not stop it. He wakes up with his heart pounding, his hands clenched into fists. He has not slept through the night in years.

His work suffers. He reads the same paragraph three times, four times, unable to hold the words. He has lost contracts because of missed deadlines. He tells himself he is just old, just tired. But he knows, in the hollow of his chest, that something broke a long time ago and never healed. He is still standing still, making himself small, waiting for a blow that will never come.
